name: ROPgadget
one_line: find ROP gadgets (useful code snippets) inside a binary
plain: `ROPgadget` searches a program for short instruction sequences that end in a return (`ret`). Each one is a gadget. In a return-oriented programming (ROP) exercise you chain gadgets so the program runs code you choose, even when the stack is not executable (NX).

A typical need: a `pop rdi ; ret` gadget to load the first argument on 64-bit Linux, then a call to `system`. ROPgadget finds the address of that gadget. Use it only on binaries from your own lab or a CTF.
when: A pwn challenge has NX on, so you cannot run shellcode from the stack.
You need the address of `pop rdi ; ret` or `syscall ; ret`.
You want to find a string like `/bin/sh` inside the binary.
You want to list every gadget and search it.

examples.title: List all gadgets
examples.explain: Prints every gadget with its address. The list is long; pipe it to grep.

examples.title: Find one gadget
examples.explain: Gives the address that loads the first function argument from the stack on x86-64.

examples.title: Only certain gadgets
examples.explain: --only keeps gadgets made of just those instructions: short, clean ones.

examples.title: Search for a string
examples.explain: Prints the address of the text in the binary if it is there.

examples.title: Look in a library
examples.explain: Libc has far more gadgets; remember to add its load address (leak it first).

examples.title: Avoid bad bytes
examples.explain: Hides gadgets whose address contains bytes your input cannot carry (a null byte or newline).

examples.title: Auto-build a chain
examples.explain: Tries to build a ready-made execve chain. It works only on simple cases; learn to build chains by hand with pwntools.

mistakes: Forgetting to add the library or PIE base: the addresses ROPgadget prints are file offsets plus the default base, not runtime addresses.
Using an address with a null byte when the vulnerable function stops at a null (strcpy, gets).
Trusting --ropchain on a real challenge: it fails often, so learn to build chains by hand.
Searching a 32-bit binary for 64-bit gadgets (check with `file`).

Search a lab libc for `/bin/sh` with --string.
Combine it with pwntools: print the gadget address and use it in a short ROP chain.
